content.text:
# ECON 101 — Week 4 Study Notes: Supply, Demand & Elasticity --- ## 1. Demand **Law of Demand:** When price rises, quantity demanded falls, *ceteris paribus* (all else held equal). → This is why the **demand curve slopes downward**. ### Determinants of demand (these SHIFT the curve) | Determinant | Example of a shift | |---|---| | **Income** | See normal vs. inferior goods below | | **Prices of related goods** | **Substitutes:** price of Coke ↑ → demand for Pepsi ↑
**Complements:** price of printers ↑ → demand for ink ↓ | | **Tastes** | A product becomes trendy → demand ↑ | | **Expectations** | Expect prices to rise next month → demand ↑ now | | **Number of buyers** | More consumers in the market → demand ↑ | ### Normal vs. inferior goods - **Normal good:** income ↑ → demand ↑ - **Inferior good:** income ↑ → demand ↓ (e.g., instant noodles) --- ## 2. Supply **Law of Supply:** When price rises, quantity supplied rises. → The supply curve slopes **upward**. ### Determinants of supply (these SHIFT the curve) - **Input prices**: inputs get cheaper → supply ↑ - **Technology**: better technology → supply ↑ - **Expectations** about future prices - **Number of sellers**: more sellers → supply ↑ --- ## 3. ⚠️ Movement Along vs. Shift of the Curve (VERY IMPORTANT) | | What causes it | What you call it | |---|---|---| | **Movement along** the curve | A change in the good's **own price** | Change in **quantity demanded / quantity supplied** | | **Shift** of the curve | A change in a **determinant** (anything except own price) | Change in **demand / supply** | **Exam trap:** "The price of coffee rose, so demand for coffee fell" is **wrong**. Correct version: *quantity demanded* fell, which is a movement along the curve. --- ## 4. Equilibrium - **Equilibrium:** where **Qd = Qs** - **Equilibrium price** is also called the **market-clearing price** | Price is... | Result | Why | |---|---|---| | **Above** equilibrium | **Surplus** | Qs > Qd | | **Below** equilibrium | **Shortage** | Qd > Qs | --- ## 5. Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) $$PED = \frac{\%\Delta Q_d}{\%\Delta P}$$ PED is usually negative because of the law of demand, so we classify it using the **absolute value**: | \|PED\| | Type | Meaning | |---|---|---| | > 1 | **Elastic** | Quantity responds strongly to price | | < 1 | **Inelastic** | Quantity barely responds to price | | = 1 | **Unit elastic** | Same proportional change | **Inelastic examples:** insulin (a necessity with no substitute), gasoline in the **short run** ### Midpoint method $$\%\Delta = \frac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{(\text{new} + \text{old})/2} \times 100$$ **Worked example:** Price goes from $4 → $6, and Qd goes from 120 → 80. - %ΔQd = (80 − 120) / 100 × 100 = **−40%** - %ΔP = (6 − 4) / 5 × 100 = **+40%** - PED = −40 / 40 = **−1** → |PED| = 1 → **unit elastic** *Why use the midpoint method?* You get the same answer whether the price goes up or down. --- ## 6. Price Controls | | Definition | Example | Binding when... | Result | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Price ceiling** | Legal **maximum** price | Rent control | Set **below** equilibrium | **Shortage** | | **Price floor** | Legal **minimum** price | Minimum wage | Set **above** equilibrium | **Surplus** | **Q from class:** *Why does a binding price ceiling cause a shortage?* **A:** At the capped price, **Qd > Qs**. The low price draws in more buyers but discourages sellers. *Memory tip:* a **ceiling** has to sit **low** (below equilibrium) to matter, and a **floor** has to sit **high** (above equilibrium) to matter. --- ## 7. Consumer & Producer Surplus - **Consumer surplus (CS)** = willingness to pay − price paid - **Producer surplus (PS)** = price received − cost - **Total surplus** = CS + PS - Total surplus is **maximized at equilibrium** --- ## ✅ Quick Self-Test (answers below) 1. Income rises and demand for bus rides falls. What kind of good are bus rides? 2. The price of pizza falls. Is this a shift of the pizza demand curve or a movement along it? 3. A new technology lowers production costs. Which curve shifts, and in which direction? 4. Price rises from $10 to $12 and Qd falls from 50 to 40. Use the midpoint method to find PED. Is demand elastic or inelastic? 5. The government sets a minimum price above equilibrium. Is there a shortage or a surplus? 6. A consumer would pay up to $15 for a ticket and pays $9. What is their consumer surplus?
Answers 1. An inferior good 2. A movement along the curve (quantity demanded rises) 3. Supply shifts right (supply increases) 4. %ΔQ = −10/45 ≈ −22.2%, %ΔP = 2/11 ≈ 18.2%, so PED ≈ −1.22. |PED| > 1, so demand is **elastic** 5. A surplus (Qs > Qd) 6. $6
--- **Study plan for the next 2 weeks:** Practise drawing the graphs (shifts, equilibrium, ceilings and floors, and the CS/PS triangles) by hand. Exams often ask you to show these on a diagram, not just define them.
